hints: Start by comparing the direction of movement with the type of molecules. Which row shows everything useful being taken back, which shows only water controlled by a hormone, and which shows a bulk movement out of the blood based on size?

Remember the three big named kidney processes that are not just diffusion or osmosis. One uses high blood pressure to push small molecules out, one reclaims all glucose selectively, and one adjusts water to control blood concentration.
Link ADH in row Q to control of blood water potential. That points to regulation of water balance, while the size limit of 68,000 in row R points to filtration through a barrier.
walkthrough:
P - Reclaiming Everything Useful**
At P, glucose, amino acids and water all move from nephron back to blood. Glucose and amino acids are 100% reclaimed in a healthy kidney because they are valuable. This selective taking back of useful solutes is called selective reabsorption.

Q - Hormone-Controlled Water Balance**
At Q, only water moves back to blood and only when ADH is present. ADH changes the permeability of the tubule to water to control blood water potential. Adjusting water loss to regulate concentration is osmoregulation.

R - Pressure Filtration By Size**
At R, water plus all small molecules below molecular mass 68,000 move from blood into the nephron. Large proteins and cells stay in blood. Forcing fluid out under high hydrostatic pressure through a filter that selects by size is ultrafiltration.
Final answer: P: selective reabsorption; Q: osmoregulation; R: ultrafiltration.

hints: Think about the order of fluid flow through the nephron. Where would fluid first enter from the blood, where would glucose first be recovered, and where would final fine-tuning of water happen?
Recall which part has microvilli and many mitochondria for reclaiming glucose, and which part has ADH-sensitive aquaporins for final water control.
Match the size filter to the cup-shaped structure around the glomerulus, and match ADH-dependent water uptake to the last part of the nephron running through the medulla.
walkthrough:
R Is First - The Filter Cup**
Fluid first leaves the blood at the glomerulus. The Bowman's capsule surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate containing water, ions, glucose, amino acids and small proteins. So R, movement from blood to nephron by size, is Bowman's capsule.

P Is Next - Reclaim All Glucose**
Just after Bowman's capsule comes the proximal convoluted tubule in the cortex. Its cells have microvilli for large surface area and many mitochondria for active uptake of glucose and amino acids by cotransport with sodium. So P, reclaiming glucose, amino acids and water, is the proximal convoluted tubule.

Q Is Last - ADH-Controlled Water**
ADH acts late in the nephron to insert aquaporins and increase water permeability. That happens mainly in the collecting duct, and also in the distal convoluted tubule. So Q, water reabsorption in presence of ADH, is the collecting duct.
Final answer: P: proximal convoluted tubule; Q: collecting duct (accept distal convoluted tubule); R: Bowman's capsule.

hints: Look at Fig. 6.1. A is the outer cortex that froze hard, B is the inner medulla that stayed softer. You are told salt concentration changes freezing point - so think which region must contain more dissolved salt.

Connect a salty medulla to kidney function. Why does the kidney deliberately build up a high salt concentration deep inside? Think about osmosis of water out of the collecting duct and the role of ADH.
walkthrough:
Salty Tissue Freezes Less Easily**
Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of a solution. Area B stayed softer and less frozen, so B must have a higher concentration of sodium chloride than A. B is the medulla and its tissue fluid, A is the cortex.

Why The Medulla Is So Salty**
The loop of Henle pumps $Na^{+}$ and $Cl^{-}$ into the medulla tissue fluid to create a steep solute gradient from cortex to medulla. This gradient draws water out of the collecting duct by osmosis as fluid flows down through the medulla, allowing concentrated urine to be produced. ADH controls this final water reabsorption, so this is part of osmoregulation.

Final answer: Region B (medulla / interstitial fluid) has higher concentration of salt / $Na^{+}$ / $Cl^{-}$, so lower freezing point and less frozen. High salt gradient draws water by osmosis from collecting duct for osmoregulation / under control of ADH.
